name: Emerging-market stress
summary: Indonesia's rupiah hit a record low near 18,390 per dollar on 26 Nov despite rate rises; no EM default or IMF rescue
state: The rupiah hit a record low of about 18,390 per dollar on 26 Nov and was heading for a third weekly fall on 27 Nov, down nearly 10% this year (Trading Economics). Bank Indonesia raised its policy rate by 25bp to 6% on 18 Nov, taking rises since May to 125bp, and continues to intervene (New Straits Times). The fall is gradual, well short of 10% in a month, and no major emerging economy in default, imposing capital controls or seeking emergency IMF support was found as of 27 Nov, so the level stays Normal.
for_you: Exposed are Indonesian importers and borrowers with dollar debts, and holders of rupiah assets. A stronger dollar and higher US rates tend to pressure other emerging-market currencies too.
rubric_hit: Normal: rupiah down ~10% this year but under 10% in a month; no EM default, capital controls or IMF emergency request

sources.title: Trading Economics — Rupiah weakens near record low
New Straits Times — Indonesia central bank hikes rates to support rupiah

why: Energy-importing and heavily indebted emerging economies crack first in oil shocks and strong-dollar periods, with knock-on defaults and unrest.
drivers: Oil and food import bills, dollar strength, FX reserves, debt maturities, IMF programmes.

rubric.alert: A sovereign default or capital controls in a major emerging economy, or several in crisis at once.
rubric.watch: A major emerging economy's currency falls more than 10% in a month, its reserves fall fast, or it seeks emergency IMF support.
rubric.normal: No major emerging economy in acute currency or debt distress.
